Sochocin Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Sochocin, Poland

Not demolished. Jewish settlement in Sochocin developed after Poland's partitions; population grew from 67 (1808) to 624 by 1857, declining to 406 by 1921. Many local Jews made and sold shell buttons for a living. Germans deported all Jewish residents in the war's early months, most dying in subsequent years. This cemetery is first documented in 1861 correspondence regarding Sochocin Jews' independence from Płońsk's synagogue supervision; an 1863 government report described it as '68½ ells long and 48½ ells wide, fenced, and founded thanks to voluntary donations.' Wartime and postwar destruction removed the fence and nearly all tombstones; damaged stones survived until at least the 1960s, though only fragments remained by 2016. A 2016-2018 restoration by the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage, ESJF, and the US Commission for the Preservation of America's Heritage Abroad added a concrete prefabricated wall, information boards, and a plaque listing those buried there, initiated by descendants of Icchak Kawa (Isidore Berenstein).
